articles.title: The Dodgers had neither the roster need nor the financial appetite to acquire Tarik Skubal
articles.summary: The Dodgers reportedly didn't make Skubal an official offer before he signed with the Mets.
articles.body:
Over the past five years, it has been rare that the Dodgers have not come out on top in the premier free-agent sweepstakes. Fans of all teams have gotten used to the Dodgers wasting little time and flexing their economic might to sign the best players, making Los Angeles home for many of the game's biggest stars.

But this week, the Los Angeles Dodgers have been reminded how it feels to be one of the 29 teams that miss out on a big-time free agent. On Sunday, L.A. watched superstar free agent Tarik Skubal take his talents to Queens, signing a record-breaking, nine-year, $450 million deal with the New York Mets .

Is Skubal signing with the Mets a shock? No, not in the slightest. But what might surprise some fans in the fallout of the historic signing is that the team that has seemed inevitable when it comes to acquiring elite players wasn't really close this time.

After acquiring Skubal at the trade deadline, the Dodgers had the opportunity to court the new $450 million man over the final months of the 2026 season. And it was clear Skubal made a great impression on the franchise.

"He was awesome getting to know [this season]. Fit in great in the clubhouse," Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said earlier this month at the GM meetings. "Obviously, we know what kind of pitcher he is."

Having the chance to showcase to Skubal what the Dodgers have built over the past decade was certainly an advantage for L.A. But in free agency, every team has an opportunity to make their pitch. And once a guy walks out the door, all bets are off that they'll return — even to a team like the Dodgers.

As it turned out, the Dodgers reportedly didn't make Skubal an official offer before he signed with the Mets.

In this round of high-stakes free agency, two key factors skewed the outcome toward the Mets over the Dodgers. The first was team need — or, you might call it desperation.

New York has long needed an ace to lead its starting rotation, and with the best ace in baseball available, it made sense that the Mets would do everything possible to acquire him. The Dodgers, on the other hand, have been building a stable of aces over the past four years led by Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Adding Skubal unquestionably strengthened what was a seemingly unstoppable group and one of, if not the best rotation in baseball.

But even without Skubal, the Dodgers have arguably the best starting quartet in the sport. So while their interest in retaining the former Tigers hurler was real, L.A.'s need for the two-time Cy Young winner wasn't nearly as great as New York's.

The second big advantage the Mets had over the Dodgers was financial certainty. The Dodgers have never been shy about their willingness to spend big, and they've drawn the ire of the rest of baseball by exercising their economic might. After signing Ohtani to his then-record $700 million deal, they continued to add to their massive payroll, which includes high-paid stars such as Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Will Smith, Snell, Glasnow and Yamamoto. In fact, the Dodgers have committed more than $2.3 billion to those 10 players, with much of it coming in the past three years.

But over the past few offseasons, L.A. has seemed a little more hesitant about signing long-term deals with large total values. Even when acquiring more star players in Díaz and Tucker, the Dodgers opted for shorter-term, higher-annual-value deals.

That's something Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, simply weren't in the market for. No, this deal was always going to be high-value and long-term.

As was shown when Juan Soto hit the market, if Mets owner Steve Cohen wants a player, he's going to get that player. This winter, the only real question was what the final number would be. We now know it was $450 million, breaking both the total value and average annual value ($50 million) records for a starting pitcher.

For the first time in a long time, the Dodgers showed that they do have limits, and Skubal's asking price surpassed them.

It also can't be ignored that team owner and chairman Mark Walter is facing federal investigations of insurance fraud and investor lawsuits, which have led him to sell significant assets across his sports portfolio. Those include recent sales of the Los Angeles Lakers, the Los Angeles Sparks and his shares in Premier League power Chelsea FC. He has also reportedly been looking to offload his Cadillac F1 team shares.

While Walter and his TWG Global holding company have been adamant that the Dodgers will not be sold, it's difficult to imagine the uncertainty surrounding the team owner's financial situation not having some kind of impact on the business operations of the team.

The Dodgers are still built to be World Series contenders for the foreseeable future, and given the superstar talent on the roster, thinking that they aren't one of baseball's best teams entering 2027 would be foolish. But if there's a lesson to be learned from Skubal's decision, it's that the almighty dollar still reigns supreme, and generational talents require generational contracts.

This time around, the Dodgers chose not to play.

articles.title: Trevor Rogers' Cubs Contract Revealed in MLB Rumors, Updated Payroll and Pitching Rotation
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs have reportedly added to their pitching staff by reaching a multiyear deal with free-agent starter Trevor Rogers on Monday, per MLB Network's Jon Morosi.
articles.body:
The Chicago Cubs have reportedly added to their pitching staff by reaching a multiyear deal with free-agent starter Trevor Rogers on Monday, per MLB Network's Jon Morosi.

According to Spotrac , he joins a Cubs team that has a projected cash payroll of $155.6 million for 2027.

He could also slide right into the top of their rotation with Cade Horton recovering from Tommy John surgery:

Rogers has quietly been one of the most valuable pitchers in MLB over the past two seasons with the Baltimore Orioles. His 7.3 fWAR during that period ranks seventh among all AL pitchers with at least 250 innings.

The 2026 season saw Rogers set career-highs in starts (30), innings (169.2) and strikeout-to-walk ratio (4.03). He tied his career-high with 157 strikeouts.

It didn't start out looking like Rogers was going to have that kind of success. His ERA was at 6.96 through his first nine starts, but the left-hander rebounded with a 3.05 ERA over his final 21 outings.

Rogers has had a fascinating career arc starting with a runner-up finish in the 2021 NL Rookie of the Year voting after posting a 2.64 ERA and 157 strikeouts in 133 innings for the Miami Marlins.

The next three years saw Rogers struggle, lose his job in the rotation and eventually get traded to Baltimore midway through the 2024 campaign.

After starting the 2025 season on the injured list due to a knee injury, Rogers debuted in May and had arguably the best year of his career. He finished with a 1.81 ERA in 109.2 innings, second-best in MLB among all pitchers with at least 100 innings.

There's a high level of risk to this deal for the Cubs because of how inconsistent Rogers has been throughout his career, but the upside that he has shown for most of the past two seasons suggests he can transform their rotation in 2027.

Few playoff contenders were screaming out for a major addition to their pitching staff than the Cubs.

Chicago's projected rotation before the Rogers signing was led by Justin Steele returning after missing almost two full seasons stemming from Tommy John surgery in April 2025. Edward Cabrera, Braxton Garrett and Javier Assad were the other projected starters in the group.

The Cubs don't need an elite-level rotation because the lineup, led by reigning NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, can score runs in bunches. But they needed to come out of this offseason with some reliable arms.

Rogers certainly comes with his own level of volatility, but he is going to step in as their best starter as things stand right now.

articles.title: Forecasting MLB's Biggest Bombshells of 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: The MLB lockout is coming. Unless either the owners or the players back off from their fight over a salary cap, there's not a darn thing anyone can do about it.
articles.body:
The MLB lockout is coming. Unless either the owners or the players back off from their fight over a salary cap, there's not a darn thing anyone can do about it.

So even if Tarik Skubal's $450 million contract with the New York Mets is the biggest move any team makes this offseason, you can still expect a lot to happen in this last week before the CBA expires on December 1.

We've come to forecast the biggest bombshells still waiting to be dropped. Everything is on the table, including trades, free-agent signings and even one shocking move that won't happen before the lockout goes into effect.

A lot of this is based on reading various tea leaves out there in the rumor mill. Some of it was also plain ol' gut feeling.

Randy Arozarena Won't Sign By the Lockout

Writing on November 18, Jeff Passan of ESPN pretty much spelled this one out: "The biggest name not to sign before the lockout could be outfielder Randy Arozarena."

If this were a normal offseason, it would be just as easy to predict that Arozarena wouldn't sign until January at the earliest. He is a Scott Boras client, after all, and Boras is famously willing to play the long game when he gets his top guys to free agency. It doesn't always work, but it does more often than not.

Even though this isn't a normal offseason, you'd swear someone forgot to tell Boras.

Per Ryan Divish and Adam Jude of The Seattle Times , Boras' target for Arozarena's contract is in the range of six years and $150 million. Even if Arozarena is a three-time All-Star, it's an aggressive ask for a 31-year-old whose bat has been slowing down. That's reason enough for teams to balk at Arozarena's market. Then add his ties to qualifying offer-related penalties.

Granted, you ask for six years and $150 million because you might be willing to settle for four years and $100 million. The distance between those two poles, however, seems too large to reckon in just a week's time.

The Phillies Will Break the Ice on Jarren Duran

Despite the near-constant trade buzz, there was some intrigue before Friday's deadline as to whether the Boston Red Sox would simply non-tender Jarren Duran.

That they didn't do that implies that they believe he still has real trade value, even with a 0.4-rWAR season in his immediate past. They're right about that. Duran was an MVP-caliber performer as recently as 2024. He still has two seasons of club control left.

According to Chris Cotillo and Sean McAdam of MassLive.com, the Houston Astros and San Diego Padres have had heavy interest in Duran in the past. Yet neither is a sure thing to trade for him now. The Astros are under new front-office leadership, while the Friars need pitching far more than they need a left fielder.

The Seattle Mariners and Philadelphia Phillies are otherwise "poking around" Duran. While neither is an ideal fit for the 30-year-old, the Phillies could use someone with a chip on his shoulder as big as Duran's. For what it's worth, the Red Sox drafted him under Dave Dombrowski's leadership in 2018.

Adding the lefty-hitting Duran would only heighten the Phillies' need for a right-handed bat, but they have some solid platoon options in free agency. As for Boston's return, a Duran-for-Orion Kerkering deal has sounded like a fun challenge trade for a while now.

The Cubs Will Be the Ones that End Up with Teruaki Sato

Speaking of Jarren Duran, there's another solid fit for him on the North Side of Chicago, where Patrick Mooney of The Athletic says the Cubs have evaluated Duran as a change-of-scenery candidate.

But that's also the less interesting part of that report, at least when compared to Mooney's sources indicating that the Cubs have "extensively scouted" Teruaki Sato.

As much as everyone is rightfully concerned about the Cubs' starting pitching, they also need to fret about an outfield currently missing Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ. That's an invite to get at least one impact bat. They're ultimately a terrific fit for Sato.

They could use another left-handed bat. They have enough depth to absorb whatever swing-and-miss comes with his prodigious power. If Sato is more likely to end up on the grass than stay at third base, there's no better place to play than next to Pete Crow-Armstrong.

Cost is still another reason Sato looks like a good fit for the Cubs. Projections for his next deal tend to max out around $100 million. Even with the posting fee that would have to go to the Hanshin Tigers, the total cost of such a contract would probably still be going to come in under what it would take to re-sign Suzuki.

Worst-Case Scenario for Each MLB Team in Offseason 😨

The Yankees Will Add Brandon Lowe and Casey Schmitt to Their Infield

In pretty much the blink of an eye, the New York Yankees got their bullpen sorted. David Bednar, Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga? That'll do.

Now they need to turn to their infield, which has an obvious hole at third base and an opening for an upgrade at second base. The latter is perhaps an obvious fit for Brandon Lowe, which should be the point of signing him.

The 32-year-old does have some bust potential , but his defensive improvement seems legit and his swing is too perfect for Yankee Stadium. Among lefty hitters who had at least 400 batted-ball events in 2026, only Pete Crow-Armstrong pulled a higher rate of fly balls to right field.

As to the hot corner, Jon Morosi of MLB Network reported that the Yankees checked in on Maikel Garcia before he landed in Seattle. Casey Schmitt and he had been name-checked as infielders on the trade block by ESPN's Jeff Passan , specifically with regard to the San Francisco Giants' hunt for starting pitching.

Frankly, Schmitt is as good a Plan B for Garcia as any. If the Yankees pitched an offer of Will Warren plus more (Jasson Domínguez, perhaps), they should get a "yes" from Buster Posey.

The Mariners Will Win the Seiya Suzuki Sweepstakes

There's an awful lot of smoke surrounding the San Diego Padres and Seiya Suzuki, with ESPN's Jeff Passan positing that they "could be the favorites" for him.

Yet when Joe Musgrove is your projected No. 1 starter at this stage of his career, well, that's a problem. Even if the pursuit ultimately failed, the fact that the Padres were even in on Tarik Skubal shows they understand this and are prioritizing accordingly.

For their part, the Seattle Mariners are a less likely fit for Suzuki based on their recent history. In a decade under Jerry Dipoto, they haven't handed out a nine-figure contract to a hitter in free agency. Why change now?

Well, because they both can and should. It would be a mistake to leave Randy Arozarena's shoes unfilled. Suzuki offers similar offensive upside but with better outfield defense. After adding Maikel Garcia in a trade with the Kansas City Royals last week, the Mariners filled their other major offensive hole without sacrificing any payroll flexibility.

The interest in Suzuki is there in Seattle, according to Adam Jude of The Seattle Times . With as much as $30-35 million still left to add to their 2027 payroll, the Mariners can add Suzuki on even a $25 million-per-year contract and still have money for other projects.

The Padres Will Reel in Michael King *and* Freddy Peralta

Speaking of the Padres' pursuit of Tarik Skubal, it says a lot that one never felt comfortable ruling them out on actually signing him. After all, new owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones are rather famously "all in."

Yet Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic raised a good point on Foul Territory : "Can they do Skubal when they need multiples?"

Indeed. In this case, they should be able to bring back Michael King and add Freddy Peralta for a lot less than it would have cost to sign Skubal.

King is just an obvious fit in San Diego, to the point where he'd be foolish to go anywhere else if he cares about his numbers. As Rosenthal and Will Sammon reported in The Athletic , the Padres are also among the teams interested in Peralta.

The Padres' projected 2027 payroll is already just $9 million short of what they spent in 2026, so money would seem to be a question mark here. If Feliciano and Jones are willing to spend more like the late Peter Seidler, maybe not.

The Dodgers Steal Adrian Morejon from the Padres

Adrian Morejon returning to the Padres already feels unlikely. It'll be that much harder to imagine if they drop a couple hundred million on Michael King and Freddy Peralta.

Fortunately for Morejon, he doesn't need the Padres to be involved to have a strong market. There's smoke around him with the Mariners and Marlins. And who knows? Maybe the Yankees are still interested even after securing David Bednar, Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga.

And yet, Morejon just feels like a future Dodger, doesn't he? And perhaps especially now that the Tarik Skubal sweepstakes have ended with someone else as the winner.

The Dodgers were a player in the sweepstakes, but their reported interest in a shorter contract (per Katie Woo of The Athletic ) probably took them out of the running well before Skubal opted for nine years and $450 million from the Mets. Besides, it's not like he ever needed a shorter deal to set an AAV record for a pitcher.

Besides, the Dodgers arguably need Morejon more. Their pen has already lost Evan Phillips and stands to lose Alex Vesia as well. After the year he had, it seems unwise to count on much from Edwin Díaz.

The Toronto Blue Jays Will Land Ketel Marte

Here's the thing about Ketel Marte's trade market: Because of his 10-and-5 rights, he'll only go anywhere if he wants to.

True to form, Marte isn't exactly making things easy. Nick Piecoro of The Arizona Republic reported that the team's brass met with Marte's agent, Charisse Espinosa-Dash, during the GM Meetings, "but did not seem to come away with a clear idea about which teams Marte would be willing to approve a deal."

Even so, there has been buzz about the Orioles poking around the three-time All-Star. The Toronto Blue Jays are also said to have interest, though Keegan Matheson of MLB.com writes that "they're not about to overextend themselves at the current ask."

Given Marte's age (33) and less-than-glamorous recent history , this is certainly the right way to go about this particular pursuit. Even if the $76 million he has left on his contract isn't too much for a player of his ilk, it doesn't exactly help Arizona's negotiating leverage. They just don't hold the cards here.

One can imagine the Blue Jays talking the Snakes into a trade that would favor Toronto, in which case the only hurdle left would be convincing Marte to OK the deal. To this end, they have the money to sweeten his remaining contract. Perhaps just as importantly, they have a well-known reputation for treating their players very well .

The Braves Will Pull Off a Trade for Logan Webb

Before this past weekend, the notion that the San Francisco Giants would trade Logan Webb seemed unlikely to the point of being laughable.

Well, then Robert Murray of FanSided reported that the Giants are open to listening on the ace right-hander. Adding to the situation, Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon of The Athletic highlighted how much more a Webb trade could add to the Giants' farm system than deals involving Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman or Willy Adames.

Among the pitching-needy teams, the Cubs and Orioles loom as potentially good fits for Webb and solid trading partners for the Giants. There's also the Braves, who badly need another top-of-the-rotation starter to pair with Chris Sale.

To that end, the Braves' relatively sparse history of free-agent signings generally makes them a better bet to add impact players in trades. Beyond being a three-time All-Star, Webb offers the appeal of being under contract for $47 million through 2028. That's more than a fair rate for an ace pitcher.

One fun concept would have Spencer Strider return to San Francisco as a change-of-scenery candidate and, for Atlanta, a salary dump. But he'd obviously need to be accompanied by prospects, perhaps including the two best Atlanta has: outfielder Eric Hartman and left-hander Cam Caminiti.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: The Worst-Case Scenario for Every MLB Team This Offseason
articles.summary: Every team and fanbase enters the offseason imagining the best-case scenario. Few actually have that plan come to fruition.
articles.body:
Every team and fanbase enters the offseason imagining the best-case scenario. Few actually have that plan come to fruition.

Obviously, this offseason will be even more complicated with the owners expected to lock the players out when the current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. We don't know when a new CBA will be in place, and what the rules will be when it is. It is not a fun time to be a president of baseball operations or a general manager.

While we're on the theme of uncertainty and negativity, here is the worst-case scenario for every MLB team this offseason.

Cleveland Guardians: Steven Kwan is traded for a piece that doesn't immediately help them

Steven Kwan hit .353 after the All-Star break, getting back on track after almost a calendar year of offensive struggles. If Kwan—who is also one of the best defensive outfielders in the game—has a strong year at the plate in 2027, it stands to reason that he could be looking for $100+ million next offseason as a free agent.

History tells us that the Guards are unlikely to meet that asking price, so it might make sense to maximize the return for the four-time Gold Glove Award winner this offseason.

With Jo Adell also in the fold and Chase DeLauter seemingly on the cusp of stardom, Cleveland's lineup could withstand the loss of Kwan better than they may have been able to a year ago.

Still, this is a team that has been to the ALCS twice in the last three years. If they trade Kwan, it needs to be for a player or package that can immediately help Stephen Vogt's club try to get to the Fall Classic in 2027, whether that's in the outfield or elsewhere.

Chicago White Sox: Dustin May can't stay healthy

The 4.70 ERA that Dustin May posted over 145.2 regular-season innings between the St. Louis Cardinals and Milwaukee Brewers this past season doesn't stand out.

However, May did post a 3.63 FIP in 2026, so the White Sox seem to be betting that the best is yet to come by giving the righty a three-year, $52.5 million contract.

We'll see if that aspect of the bet works out, but the biggest concern regarding the 2016 third-round pick has to be his durability. He logged a grand total of 295.2 innings during parts of seven years with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The biggest risk here isn't that May ends up being an overpaid No. 4 starter, but rather that he just can't stay on the mound.

Minnesota Twins: Sonny Gray finally hits a wall

Props to new control person Tom Pohlad, who seems to be putting his money where his mouth is.

Days after Ryan Jeffers accepted the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer, the Twins brought back Sonny Gray in free agency on a two-year, $55 million deal. Gray—who previously pitched for the Twins from 2022-2023—led the American League with 18 wins this past season, finishing fifth in Cy Young Award voting after posting a 2.72 ERA in what turned out to be his lone season with the Boston Red Sox.

Theoretically, a rotation with Gray, Joe Ryan and Taj Bradley—with Pablo López returning from Tommy John surgery at some point—could be really good. The question is just how much longer Gray, 37, can pitch at this level. It would be very deflating if the first season of a two-year deal is when the three-time All-Star finally hits a wall.

Detroit Tigers: They don't add an impact veteran bat

The Tigers entered 2026 with World Series aspirations. Instead, they turned out to be one of the sport's most disappointing teams, going 76-86.

With Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize traded midseason and Jack Flaherty now a free agent, you can make the argument that the No. 1 priority for the Tigers needs to be to add another quality starter. Emilio Pagán did just get a one-year, $11.5 million deal from Detroit, although Scott Harris might also be inclined to add another late-inning reliever before the offseason is out.

Yet, it feels like the Tigers need to land a veteran bat. It's hard to imagine going into the 2027 season with Hao-Yu Lee, Colt Keith and Ben Malgeri all projected to get major at-bats. Detroit could sign any of Luis Arraez, Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Brandon Lowe to replace Gleyber Torres at second base, rather than handing the job to Lee. Alternatively, the Tigers could trade former No. 1 overall pick Spencer Torkelson and sign a veteran option at first base like Ty France.

Kansas City Royals: Fail to add an outfield bat

Even though former first-round pick Jac Caglianone had a breakout season with an .834 OPS, the Royals still finished 23rd among all teams in outfield OPS at .698.

By virtue of Caglianone's emergence, the Royals are in a better place with their outfield than they were a year ago. Still, it seems like we've been talking about a lack of impact bats in their outfield for years now. President of baseball operations J.J. Picollo needs to find an impact bat for at least one of the two other spots in his outfield this offseason.

Defensive-first center fielder Kyle Isbel was already non-tendered. As things stand right now, Roster Resource has rookie Carson Roccaforte penciled in as their starting center fielder and the left-handed hitting John Rave in left field. That alone probably isn't going to cut it. An interesting option could be for the Royals to work out a trade with the Los Angeles Dodgers to bring in Teoscar Hernández . Admittedly, they would have to put up with some shortcomings defensively, but Hernández still posted a .907 OPS against lefties last year. If the Dodgers would be willing to eat a portion of the $17.34 million owed to Hernández in 2027, he would make sense for the Royals.

Tampa Bay Rays: Starting pitching staff has massive talent drain

The Rays won the AL pennant this past year, doing so with a rotation that was pretty strong in the postseason despite being without Shane McClanahan.

However, it does appear they could lose two of their key postseason starters. B/R has ranked Freddy Peralta as the No. 9 free agent this offseason, and Nick Martinez as No. 21, projecting both will depart Tampa Bay in free agency.

It seems as though the Rays will hold onto Drew Rasmussen for his contract year, but he has an injury history and will be pretty expensive next offseason, so you can never be sure. McClanahan is a two-time All-Star, but has logged just 118 innings over the last three seasons.

Erik Neander and the Rays are used to their roster having quite a bit of year-to-year turnover, but they do run the risk of just not having enough arms in 2027 depending on how this offseason plays out.

New York Yankees: Unable to find corner infield bat

Brian Cashman needs to find a corner infield bat, likely a right-handed hitting one, this winter.

Luis García Jr. did hit 30 home runs between the Washington Nationals and Yankees this past year, but posted just a .653 OPS against left-handed pitching. Meanwhile, the left-handed hitting Ryan McMahon was just straight up bad at the plate in 2026, hitting just .213 in 328 at-bats.

The need for a right-handed hitting corner infielder is why the Yankees are among the clubs who have been linked to Alec Bohm this offseason. Bohm is a free agent after seven seasons with the Philadelphia Phillies that featured trials and tribulations. He would be a defensive downgrade from McMahon at third base, but has an .853 career OPS against left-handed pitching, and is a lifetime .314 hitter with runners in scoring position. His ability to play both third and first might make him a good fit for the Bronx.

Boston Red Sox: Jake Bauers can't come close to replicating 2026

If Jake Bauers replicates a 2026 campaign that saw him hit 26 home runs, drive in 86 runs and win NLCS MVP for the eventual World Series Champion Milwaukee Brewers, the four-year, $58 million deal the Red Sox gave him will be a bargain.

President of baseball operations Craig Breslow certainly took some risk in signing Bauers, however. After all, this was a player with an 84 OPS+ in 613 career games before 2026. If you watched Bauers this past year, he felt like a legitimate star. Hopefully for the Red Sox, he's not a one-year wonder.

Baltimore Orioles: They trade a former top prospect, and said prospect finally clicks elsewhere

The Orioles seemed set up to be baseball's best team in the second half of the 2020s when they had one of the more highly-touted farm systems baseball has ever seen. However, many of those young players have now reached a fork in the road for an O's team that's had consecutive underwhelming seasons:

Colton Cowser finished runner-up to Luis Gil for AL Rookie of the Year in 2024. Since posting a 120 OPS+ as a rookie, Cowser has posted a 90 OPS+ , below the league average of 100.

Jordan Westburg has a .768 OPS in parts of three MLB seasons, but missed all of 2026 due to right elbow surgery. That followed up him only appearing in 85 games in 2025.

Coby Mayo did homer 24 times in 2026, but also finished with minus-nine defensive runs saved at third base. With Pete Alonso entrenched at first base, Mayo might be a change-of-scenery candidate.

Jackson Holliday broke into the league as a 20-year-old in 2024. But the former No. 1 overall pick is just a .229 career hitter through his first 1,091 MLB at-bats.

President of baseball operations Mike Elias needs some more certainty in his lineup as he tries to avoid a third straight underwhelming season, which might be the nail in his coffin. But the fear in trading any of these pieces is that you've gone through some of the rough patches in developing them, and could be handing them over to another team to get the peak seasons.

Toronto Blue Jays: They make another major investment that goes the way of Anthony Santander

We don't yet know what it will be, but it seems like the Blue Jays are prepared to make a major transaction or two as they try to rebound from a last-place finish in the crowded AL East in 2026.

The worst thing that could happen is for that investment to go anything like how Anthony Santander's signing has so far. Toronto gave him a five-year, $92.5 million contract after he homered 44 times for the division-rival Orioles in 2024.

Over his first two years north of the border, Santander has played in just 54 games, including missing the entirety of the 2026 campaign after undergoing left shoulder surgery.

If that wasn't bad enough, Santander has made headlines this offseason for sharing anti-Muslim social media posts, prompting apologies from both him and Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro. This deal increasingly feels like a sunk cost.

Houston Astros: They don't get proper value in trade of star

Both Jeremy Peña and Isaac Paredes are entering contract years. It's possible that at this time next year, both will be looking for deals worth more than $100 million. Historically, the Astros haven't given out a ton of market-value megadeals under owner Jim Crane, just ask Gerrit Cole, Justin Verlander, Kyle Tucker and Alex Bregman.

Tucker could offer a blueprint for how the Astros act with at least one of Peña and Paredes this offseason. Rather than holding onto Tucker for his contract year in 2025, the Astros dealt him to the Chicago Cubs, acquiring Cam Smith and Paredes as part of the return. Smith hasn't yet reached the level that the Astros hoped from him, but he's still only 22. Paredes, meanwhile, hit 25 home runs and posted an .806 OPS in 2026. For one year of Tucker, the Astros did pretty well.

That will be the test for new general manager Randy Flores. If the Astros don't want to carry one or both of Peña and Paredes into their walk years, make sure you get back value that allows the team to contend in 2027 without skipping a beat. Failing to do so would be a pretty bad start to his tenure as GM.

Texas Rangers: None of their veterans waive no-trade clauses

Considering how weak the AL West was last season, there's an argument that the Rangers should try to make some tweaks this winter with the thought that they could win the division in 2027.

However, that doesn't seem to be the way things are trending, with president of baseball operations Chris Young suggesting the Rangers plan to carry a "very similar" payroll to what they had in 2026. For what it's worth, Spotrac estimates that the Rangers had a total payroll of $191.2 million in 2026, which was 13th in the sport.

If the Rangers want to make any notable external additions, they may first have to subtract some payroll on the books. Corey Seager has been mentioned as a trade candidate early this offseason, but he now has a full no-trade clause via 10-and-5 rights. Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi already had full no-trade clauses written into their contracts, with the former using his last summer to block a potential deal to the Atlanta Braves. Seager, deGrom and Eovaldi are due $92.5 million combined in 2027. Brandon Nimmo is the next highest paid player at $20.5 million, and he already waived his full no-trade clause last winter to accept a trade from the New York Mets.

It's possible that if the Rangers keep largely the same club together, they'll compete in 2027 because the AL West will be so bad. But it's clear that they would look to reallocate some of their spending. From the organization's perspective, getting stuck with veterans unwilling to move wouldn't be an ideal outcome.

Seattle Mariners: Maikel Garcia's offense falls off a cliff

Jerry Dipoto is always active, and has already pulled off a major trade, sending RHP Bryce Miller and reliever Jose A. Ferrer to the Royals in a trade that brought back, among others, third baseman Maikel Garcia.

Considering Garcia posted a .715 OPS in 82 games for Kansas City last year, the Mariners are likely aware of the reality that the .800 OPS the third baseman posted in 2025 might prove to be something of an outlier. They just have to hope that T-Mobile Park— which ranks as the least friendly hitter ballpark over the last three seasons—doesn't further sap his offensive production. Kauffman Stadium isn't thought of as a bandbox, but only four venues have a better Park Factor than the 102 "The K" has posted since the start of the 2024 season. So Garcia is going to a much worse stadium to hit at, one that even Hall of Famer Adrian Beltre never completely figured out.

If you're looking for a silver lining, Garcia's value is hardly dependent just on his output at the plate. Garcia won a Gold Glove Award in 2025, and stole 37 bases in 2024. Still, the M's have to hope he doesn't become the latest victim of T-Mobile Park, which is typically seen as a lovely stadium for everyone other than those standing in the batter's box.

Athletics: They can't attract pitching talent

Teams will often make major signings the offseason before moving into a new stadium to try to build excitement and momentum. Considering the Athletics are not only moving into a new stadium, but to a new city in 2028, you would think new president of baseball operations Taylor Smith would like to make a splash this winter.

However, the A's have to deal with the reality that for one more year, they'll still be playing their home slate at Sutter Health Park. Not only are free agents not excited to play home games at a Triple-A park, but pitchers will be particularly hesitant to sign to toe the rubber in a stadium that's been the second-most hitter-friendly park the last two years behind only Coors Field.

For all the lineup talent that the A's have, they're pretty thin on pitching. Even with a move to Las Vegas likely coming in 2028, the Athletics might have to include hazard pay to sign a free agent pitcher with options this offseason. That, or they'll have to look to acquire a controllable starter via trade.

Los Angeles Angels: Is there really anything that would qualify as a nightmare at this point?

Sure, the Angels don't have a manager, or a long-term president of baseball operations. But for a franchise that wasted having Shohei Ohtani and Mike Trout together and hasn't been to the postseason since 2014, does that really reach the level of nightmare?

A true nightmare would have been if Arte Moreno continued to own the team. Stan Kroenke's group has a mess that will likely take years to clean up, but at least that can start now.

Forecasting MLB's Biggest 2027 Bombshells 😲

Milwaukee Brewers: There really isn't anything

This isn't meant to be lazy, but the Brewers just won their first World Series title, which probably buys them a year of grace from fans.

Beyond that, the Brewers have lost Corbin Burnes, Willy Adames, Devin Williams and Peralta in recent offseasons. They've gone on without skipping a beat. So if closer Trevor Megill is traded before his contract year—on top of already losing Bauers to the Red Sox—will there really be any panic?

Heck, even in the unlikely event the Brewers become open to trading World Series MVP William Contreras before his contract year, this organization has earned the benefit of the doubt.

Chicago Cubs: They can't get a stable starting rotation together

Seiya Suzuki posted an .823 OPS in five seasons with the Cubs, so losing him would be a pretty bad outcome, particularly if there isn't a corresponding move made to try to replace his production.

Still, Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga, Clay Holmes, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson and Colin Rea are all free agents. Just with that knowledge alone, it's fair to conclude that the No. 1 priority for Jed Hoyer needs to be the starting rotation.

What's more, the remaining group of starters doesn't exactly scream durability. Justin Steele has made just four starts over the past two seasons. Edward Cabrera was limited to just 80 innings in his first year in Chicago after being acquired via trade from the Miami Marlins, and posted a 5.96 ERA in those frames.

The Cubs did start the process of rebuilding their rotation by signing Trevor Rogers to a five-year, $120 million contract with deferrals Tuesday.

Rogers is a high upside guy, and the Cubs are betting that he's closer to the version that posted a 3.52 ERA in the second half, as opposed to a 4.48 ERA in the first. But he can't be their only rotation addition.

Pittsburgh Pirates: Brandon Lowe leaves and his presence in the lineup isn't replaced

Because Brandon Lowe declined the qualifying offer from the Pirates, the Buccos will receive a compensatory pick between the first round and Competitive Balance Round A in the 2027 draft if he signs for more than $50 million with another team in free agency. The low-budget Pirates might prefer that outcome.

With that said, the Pirates are coming off of their first winning season since 2018, and Lowe was a major reason for that. After being acquired from the Rays via trade, he homered 35 times and drove in 96 runs for the Pirates, en route to winning a Silver Slugger.

There are a slew of other second basemen available in free agency, whether it's Chisholm, Arraez or Gleyber Torres. There would be some strategy in letting Lowe walk for the pick, but the Pirates then need to pivot and find another impactful lineup piece to try to make up for at least some of his presence.

St. Louis Cardinals: They pick the wrong catcher(s)

It seems that the RedBirds will not only hold onto first baseman Alec Burleson, but might look to try to extend him this offseason. Even if first basemen can be replaceable, that seems like a wise move.

There's probably not a ton Chaim Bloom can do this offseason that would come back to really burn the franchise, but he does have a looming decision to make on the team's surplus of catchers. Leo Bernal, Ivan Herrera, Pedro Pagés, Jimmy Crooks and Rainiel Rodríguez aren't going to co-exist long-term.

Pagés and Crooks seem to be the two most likely trade candidates. It's possible that the Cardinals take advantage of the dearth of catchers in baseball right now and actually turn their surplus into a positive. Whenever it feels like you have to make a decision like this, though, the worry is you pick the wrong guy(s).

Cincinnati Reds: A piece they trade clicks elsewhere

Let's assume that the Reds don't feel like they need to make a long-term decision about Elly De La Cruz—who can't become a free agent until after the 2029 season—this winter. What's the worst thing they could do this offseason?

Well, one of the things about when Bob Castellini is your owner is you probably aren't going to spend enough money to truly give out a deal that you regret. But there are a few trade candidates in Cincinnati that, like with the Orioles, you would worry about clicking elsewhere:

Matt McLain has never looked the same after left shoulder surgery cost him the entire 2024 season. Over the last two years, McLain has hit .204 with a .627 OPS. However, he's still only 27 and burst onto the scene with 16 homers and an .864 OPS in 365 at-bats as a rookie in 2023.

Nick Lodolo has garnered trade interest already this offseason, per Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic . He's struggled to consistently stay healthy, and finished 2026 with a 4.97 ERA across 21 starts. However, his best glimpses have been impressive, most notably when he pitched two complete games and posted a 3.33 ERA across a career-high 156.2 innings in 2025. Particularly with Hunter Greene likely to miss all of 2027 recovering from Tommy John surgery, trading Lodolo and seeing him click in his age-29 season elsewhere would burn.

Spencer Steer always seems to be mentioned as a trade candidate. He had a modest .739 OPS this past year, but between his .838 career OPS against lefties and positional flexibility, it's not hard to imagine Steer becoming a valuable Swiss Army knife for a contender if dealt.

Atlanta Braves: Fail to add a stable starter

Like the Cubs, the Braves not only need to add a starter this winter, but one they can be pretty sure will make 30 starts.

Spencer Schwellenbach missed all of 2026 with an elbow fracture that eventually required surgery in August. Hurston Waldrep had Tommy John surgery in September, so don't expect to see him in 2027.

Spencer Strider has made 33 total starts in the last three seasons. And while Chris Sale has been mostly healthy in three years with the Braves, he will pitch next season at 38 and Atlanta opted to give him an extra day of rest between most starts in 2026.

Logan Webb makes a ton of sense for the Braves if the San Francisco Giants are willing to listen , because not only is he a frontline starter but he also led the National League in innings pitched every year in both 2023 to 2024.

Sandy Alcantara would also be a fit, though it doesn't seem the Miami Marlins are inclined to trade him right now, especially within the division.

Philadelphia Phillies: They sign another big contract and it doesn't go well

Maybe one of the reasons that the Phillies have been so consistently tied to Teruaki Sato this offseason—as opposed to Arozarena or Suzuki—is that they are terrified of giving out another megadeal to a player on the wrong side of 30.

The Phillies still have some really productive, but expensive, veterans, such as Bryce Harper, Zack Wheeler and Kyle Schwarber. Other large contracts like Trea Turner, J.T. Realmuto and Aaron Nola don't look quite as good. Not only are the Phillies an old and expensive club, but most outlets don't rank their farm system well.

So while the Phillies don't want to waste the final years of the Harper/Wheeler/Schwarber peak, they need to strike a balance. Not only would signing Suzuki or Arozarena require giving over $100 million to a player over 30, but also giving up their second- and fifth-round picks in the 2027 draft, along with $1 million in international bonus pool money. If you're trying to get younger and develop more internally, doing that probably doesn't make sense.

It's going to be a tough balance for Dave Dombrowski, who won't want to put another questionable long-term deal to an aging player on the books.

Miami Marlins: Subtract more than they add

The Marlins say they don't plan to trade former NL Cy Young Award winner Sandy Alcantara this offseason, despite him entering a contract year. However, Barry Jackson of the Miami Herald has reported that either of the middle infield duo of Otto Lopez and Xavier Edwards could be available for "a lot."

Honestly, the Marlins should hold onto all three and try to compete in 2027. In fact, they should add onto an 80-82 club. The history of the franchise—including under current owner Bruce Sherman—suggests that route might not be likely, though.

Between Aiva Arquette and Jacob Lombard, Miami's system has some impressive middle infield pieces. They probably could withstand the loss of either Lopez or Edwards. But if any piece is traded, it needs to be for players ready to help the current club, rather than continuing to always punt towards the distant future.

Washington Nationals: Continue to be directionless

Perhaps this is an unfair way to frame things because by going 77-85 in 2026, the Nationals did overachieve. By all accounts, the Paul Taboni/Blake Butera Era is off to a strong start.

This critique is more of a big-picture one. The Nationals regularly carried top-10 (if not top-five) payrolls in the late-2010s. They were eventually rewarded with a World Series title in 2019.

Since then, however, Ted Lerner's family hasn't shown a willingness to spend like their father did. Mark Lerner flirted with selling the team in 2022, only to eventually say prior to the 2024 season that he planned to hold onto the club. But until the Nationals start spending in earnest again—it's not like D.C. is a small market—it's fair to wonder if he's still hoping to flip the club.

If Lerner is committed to the long-term success of the franchise, he should show it this offseason. CJ Abrams is two years from free agency, while James Wood is three. Rather than trading either, open up the checkbook and try to sign them to long-term deals.

New York Mets: Tarik Skubal can't stay healthy

Mets fans should feel ecstatic about the addition of Tarik Skubal. Even with Jacob Misiorowski coming off of a dominant 2026 season, many 2027 lists will still rank Skubal as the top starting pitcher in the sport.

The only real concern regarding the nine-year, $450 million deal for Skubal is durability. He underwent Tommy John surgery as a collegiate pitcher in 2017. As a member of the Tigers, he had flexor tendon surgery in 2022. And then last spring, he underwent the innovative nanoscope procedure to remove loose bodies from his elbow.

By all accounts, Skubal is healthy, and no one is suggesting he needs to make 33 starts all nine years of this deal for the contract to be successful. But there are some red flags, so if his health goes south, the Mets will end up with egg on their faces.

Los Angeles Dodgers: They don't get a plan in place to keep Shohei Ohtani healthy

The Dodgers have made it to the NLCS three times in as many years with Shohei Ohtani, winning the World Series in each of the first two campaigns. So let's keep things in perspective.

With that said, the Dodgers have had trouble getting Ohtani to the finish line in one piece in recent years. That was particularly true in October of 2026, when Ohtani struck out 10 times in 26 at-bats and was a liability. Heck, he wasn't right in September.

When healthy, Ohtani is one of the best pitchers in baseball, as evidenced by the 1.79 ERA he posted in 14 starts this past season. But having his bat healthy in October is the most important thing, even if that means cutting back on his early-season starts moving forward. As Ohtani approaches his mid-30s, the Dodgers need to find a balance between allowing him to continue being a two-way player, while also assuring that when October rolls around, he's able to be in peak form offensively.

San Diego Padres: Unable to get together a coherent starting pitching staff

Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Walker Buehler, Casey Mize and Robbie Ray are all free agents. A.J. Preller is a master at wheeling and dealing, but he has his work cut out trying to have a competent starting staff in place before next season.

Arizona Diamondbacks: Agree to a trade for Ketel Marte, but he blocks it

The Diamondbacks erred in a major way last offseason not trading Ketel Marte before he accumulated enough service time to get a full no-trade clause via 10-and-5 rights.

In theory, the $77.75 million Marte is owed over the next four seasons (plus an $11.5 million player option for 2031) shouldn't be prohibitive in trade talks. If anything, it leans toward the team-friendly side of things.

However, he did see his production dip in 2026, posting a .748 OPS after averaging an .887 OPS from 2023 to 2025. Even worse, he didn't show up for a game in August and was initially placed on the restricted list before being moved to the IL. There have been other instances of Marte not being available when expected in the past.

Further complicating things is that the Snakes don't even seem to be sure whether Marte would be willing to waive his no-trade clause if a deal could be reached, per Nick Piecoro of Arizona Republic.

The Diamondbacks would probably like to get out of the Marte business, but he holds all the cards with his NTC, and they have to be careful not to further inflame things by asking him to waive it if he doesn't want to.

San Francisco Giants: Aren't able to establish a clear direction

Do the Giants see themselves as contenders in 2027? If not, what does that say about the job that Buster Posey is doing as president of baseball operations, because he's certainly spent like someone who is trying to compete.

A willingness to listen on Webb indicates that the Giants are aware much of their roster is relatively inflexible. Moving Webb could allow them to either get back a slew of prospects who reinvigorate the system, or attach another major contract unlikely to otherwise be traded like Adames, Rafael Devers or Matt Chapman.

However, it was Posey who acquired Adames, Devers and Chapman, so if he now has to trade one of the best pitchers in franchise history to offload one of that trio, it makes you question whether the former NL MVP should be running the show in San Francisco.

In any event, the Giants need to make clear this offseason what their direction is.

Colorado Rockies: Attempts to acquire pitching fail

Paul DePodesta is trying to fix a problem that's plagued the Rockies since their inception in 1993: a lack of starting pitching.

Already, DePodesta has acquired Luis Castillo and Davis Martin from the White Sox. Castillo is definitely a bounce-back candidate after the three-time All-Star posted a 5.85 ERA between the Mariners and White Sox last year. These are the type of risks you have to take if you're the Rockies.

Also, taking back Castillo allowed the Rockies to get Martin, who pitched to a 3.95 ERA in 146 innings last year and can't become a free agent until after the 2030 campaign.

The worst-case scenario (and perhaps most likely) is that the veteran additions Colorado has made so far—with the possibility for more—don't make a meaningful impact because Coors Field is such a terrible place to pitch at.

If that proves to be the case, the Rockies won't have much room to pivot, because they're not tearing down one of the most beautiful stadiums in the sport.
